title: Facilitators exist because Executor Agents cannot interpret the Atlas themselves and must contract someone who can
content:
A.1.7 gives the Facilitator role a definition that is easy to misread as administrative: "A type of Alignment Conserver, Facilitators are contracted by Executor Agents to interpret the Atlas and Artifacts on their behalf." A.1.7.1 and A.1.7.2 make it mandatory and universal — "Every Operational Executor Agent must have a Facilitator" and "Every Core Executor Agent must have a Facilitator" — in each case via "an agreement where the Facilitator agrees to interpret the Atlas and Artifacts on behalf of the Agent."

The structural claim is that **interpretation is a service an Agent buys, not a capacity an Agent has**. Executor Agents act; interpreting what the rules require of them is delegated to a contracted human Alignment Conserver. That is a deliberate separation of execution from construal.

Why it matters follows from everything the Atlas says about interpretation elsewhere. Reading the Atlas requires grasping the spirit behind the letter (A.0.1.1.9), extrapolating where text is silent based on the interpreter's own state of Universal Alignment (A.1.1.2.0.3.1), and keeping inferences "maximally grounded" in explicit language (A.1.5.3.0.3.2). Those are judgment operations that the framework treats as requiring an aligned actor who can be held accountable — which an Agent, as a mechanism, cannot be.

So the mandatory pairing is an accountability bridge: for every Agent taking action, there is a named AC who owns the interpretation behind it and who is subject to the full AC regime — single-role restriction, anonymity, 51% derecognition threshold, inverted burden of proof. The Agent executes; the Facilitator is answerable for what the rules were understood to mean.

This also explains why Facilitator opsec (A.1.7.3) is framed in terms of "physical risk posed by the potential for attacks against Facilitators": whoever controls a Facilitator controls how the Atlas is read for that Agent.
